issue: Can a state court's exclusion of defense evidence under a discretionary evidentiary rule be an unreasonable application of the Supreme Court's complete-defense cases (Chambers and Crane) under AEDPA, or do those cases reach only categorical exclusion rules?

sides.position: Applying a discretionary evidentiary rule to exclude defense evidence does not violate the right to present a complete defense, so a state court's ruling to that effect is not an unreasonable application of Crane or Chambers.
cases: Troy v. Sec'y, Fla. Dep't of Corr., 763 F.3d 1305 (11th Cir. 2014)

sides.position: A state court can unreasonably apply Crane and Chambers when it excludes critical defense evidence under a discretionary rule, so the complete-defense right is not limited to categorical exclusion rules.

quote: Therefore, even if this case concerned a "discretionary evidence rule" (which it does not), our holding that the state habeas court unreasonably applied Crane and Chambers would not create a circuit split— the Ninth Circuit has already done so with a decision inconsistent with seven other circuits, including ours.
